records.p: The Eastern Grass Owl has a broad facial disc, long legs and a slender, long-winged appearance. Adults have a pale buff to whitish disc and underparts, with females on average more richly buff and more strongly spotted than males. Compared with Barn Owls, Grass Owls have relatively long legs and reduced feathering over the lower tarsus and toes (Australian Bird Study Association, n.d.). The Eastern Grass Owl is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Tagubud, and Davao del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Eastern Grass Owl is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats and cultivated land.

An exceptionally long slender neck, sharply pointed bill and white streaks on the folded dark wings identify this darter (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Oriental Darter has been documented on Mindanao, including Lake Lanao and Lanao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Darter is broadly associated with forests, freshwater wetlands. An early account recorded breeding around Lake Naujan, Mindoro, and use of freshwater streams elsewhere on that island (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Adult males are black with a white patch on each flank, while adult females show a broad white breast and collar (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Lesser Frigatebird has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Lesser Frigatebird is associated with shrublands, coastal and intertidal habitats, and offshore waters. Historical observers encountered birds flying singly or in small flocks over Philippine marine waters (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The Great Frigatebird is a large, long-winged seabird with sharply bent, pointed wings, a hooked bill and a deeply forked tail. Adult males are nearly black and show a red inflatable throat sac in display; adult females have a contrasting white breast. Young birds have extensive white on the head, neck and breast. The folded tail can look pointed in flight (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.). The Great Frigatebird has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Great Frigatebird is broadly associated with shrubland, coastal and intertidal habitats, and marine waters. AVONET lists a culmen length of 116.8 mm, wing length of 567.8 mm, tail length of 396.5 mm, and body mass of 1274.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Little Black Cormorant is a compact, all-dark cormorant, with entirely black plumage and conspicuous green eyes in adult birds. It is much smaller than a Great Cormorant and lacks the white underside of the similar-sized Little Pied Cormorant (Australian Museum, n.d.). The Little Black Cormorant is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Little Black Cormorant is associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and other open or cultivated landscapes in the regional working checklist. AVONET lists a culmen length of 51.9 mm, wing length of 248.8 mm, tail length of 128.8 mm, and body mass of 995 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: Adults have dark chocolate-brown head, chest, upperparts and wings sharply divided from a white belly (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Brown Booby has records from Mindanao, Bohol, and Siargao (GBIF.org, 2026). Brown Boobies capture fish and squid in headfirst plunge dives into the sea (National Audubon Society, n.d.). The Brown Booby is associated with coastal and intertidal habitats as well as offshore waters. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 79.3 mm, wing length of 366.8 mm, tail length of 193.8 mm, and body mass of 1031.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Red-footed Booby is recorded in the Zamboanga Peninsula of western Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Red-footed Booby is broadly associated with marine waters.

The male Philippine Trogon has a deep reddish-purple crown, black forehead and throat, bright scarlet breast and belly, orange-brown upperparts and finely barred black wings. Its outer tail feathers are extensively white with black bases. The female lacks the purple crown and scarlet underside, showing an olive-brown head and upperparts with buff underparts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Trogon has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Trogon is associated with forests.

A multilocus phylogeographic study detected deeply divergent Mindanao Ansonia lineages, including cryptic lineages in western Mindanao (Sanguila et al., 2011). AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 50 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The McGregor's Slender Stream Toad has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Pasonanca area, Zamboanga del Norte, and Zamboanga del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011; AMNH Amphibian Species of the World, n.d.; AMNH, n.d.; Nuñeza et al., 2010). McGregor’s Stream Toad is associated with mountain forests and streams in central and western Mindanao. Unresolved lineages within the wider Ansonia complex limit how broadly this summary can be applied (Frost, 2026). Studies of advertisement calls in the Mindanao Ansonia complex indicate geographic variation and potentially undescribed lineages (AMNH Amphibian Species of the World, n.d.; AMNH, n.d.). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial, aquatic and arboreal, with larval development (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 38 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Müller's Slender Stream Toad is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Lumot, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). Its stream-dwelling larvae require fast-flowing water, linking populations to mountain torrents and nearby forest (Sanguila et al., 2016). Mt. Hilong-hilong surveys documented specimens on forest-floor leaf litter, in rocky crevices and along stream banks between about 700 and 1,300 m (Sanguila et al., 2016). Historical and recent voucher-based records from the Taguibo Watershed in Butuan City place this toad on ground surfaces in the sampled riparian and terrestrial zones (Sanguila et al., 2021). A stomach-content study of stream-associated amphibians in northeastern Mindanao found that ants predominated in the diet of Müller’s Slender Stream Toad (Plaza et al., 2021). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A small toad with webbing on the first finger, indistinct tympanum and dark throat markings (Plaza et al., 2025). The Western Mindanao Toadlet has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Tubluka, Mount Sinaka, and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Sanguila et al., 2016). The Western Mindanao Toadlet has been observed on leaves of saplings and shrubs near streams, including forest edges and other moderately disturbed areas. Some populations remain subject to taxonomic review (Plaza et al., 2025; Sanguila et al., 2016; Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Toadlets examined from northeastern Leyte had a reported mean snout–vent length of 16.15 ± 0.62 mm (Decena et al., 2023). The Eastern Mindanao Toadlet has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Mount Sinaka, Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, and Zamboanga del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; AMNH, n.d.; Diesmos et al., 2026; Frost, 2026). The Eastern Mindanao Toadlet has been observed on low ferns and shrub leaves in montane forest in the Leyte Cordillera (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe this toad as using both ground-level and arboreal habitats and undergoing larval development (Oliveira et al., 2017). It was originally described as Nectophryne lighti from the Mindanao region in 1920 (AMNH, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Parotoid glands behind the eyes and a brown, warty back distinguish this toad (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Cane Toad is widely recorded across Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol and Dinagat. Mindanao localities include the Mount Kitanglad Range, Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Mount Lumot and Mount Agad-Agad, while Samar records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Sanguila et al., 2016; Maglangit et al., 2022; Beukema, 2011). Philippine herpetofaunal surveys document the species in human-modified environments, including agricultural and settled landscapes (Sanguila et al., 2016). In Agusan Marsh it was recorded around agricultural margins and mixed freshwater-swamp vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2026). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in ground-level habitats (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe the Cane Toad as using terrestrial and aquatic habitats, undergoing larval development, and feeding on arthropods and some vertebrates. Activity is reported by day and night (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: Adults described from eastern Samar have markedly expanded digital discs, large eyes, spotted flanks and sparse salmon-colored dorsal tubercles. Nine males measured 34.2–39.1 mm snout–vent length and nine females 44.3–49.8 mm (Siler et al., 2009). The Walter's Limestone Forest Frog has been documented on Samar, including Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Frost, 2026). Walter’s Limestone Forest Frog inhabits the forest floor and terrestrial limestone habitats of eastern Samar (Siler et al., 2009). The name is based on an eastern Samar type series from Taft Forest at about 140 m, and was originally placed in the Platymantis guentheri group. The diagnostic identity is tied to these vouchers; superficial similarity to other local wrinkled frogs is insufficient for unvouchered records (Frost, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The study describes conspicuous dorsolateral folds and long dorsal ridges in frogs approximately 35–50 mm long (Plaza et al., 2025). The northeastern Leyte account describes variable brown, grey, or black facial-mask coloration and elongate tubercular ridges along the back as useful identification characters (Decena et al., 2023). The Masked Wrinkled Ground Frog has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; Beukema, 2011). In the Taguibo Watershed survey, specimens identified as Platymantis corrugatus were recorded on ground-level habitats in the terrestrial zone away from immediate stream margins. This is a site-specific habitat-use record (Sanguila et al., 2021). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in ground-level habitats (Decena et al., 2023). Mindanao populations assigned to this species complex were observed calling from exposed sites through the evening (Sanguila et al., 2016). In northeastern Leyte, males called from leaf litter and ground surfaces at night; their calls were sometimes heard from concealed sites during the day after rain (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial, and indicate direct development without a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 35 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Günther's Wrinkled Tree Frog has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026). At Agusan Marsh, calling individuals perched above peat-swamp ground on vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2026). In Agusan peat-swamp forest, individuals called from vegetation approximately 1–3 m above the ground (Sanguila et al., 2026). Calling males in the Leyte forest survey were generally detected on fern leaves, small branches, or other vegetation within about 1 m of the ground (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and arboreal, and indicate direct development without a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The 2026 original species treatment diagnoses a moderate-sized, broad-headed, terrestrial forest frog (reported specimen snout–vent length 26.7–39.9 mm; mean 33.9 mm), with unexpanded finger and toe tips, conspicuously raised subarticular tubercles, and rugose dorsal skin bearing rounded tubercles or short, irregular ridges. There may be up to six longitudinal or oblique dorsal ridges, although some specimens lack them. Background color varies from chestnut to dull brown, sometimes with thick dorsolateral markings. Compared with its sister species P. jagorii, the published sample is generally larger and has different proportional measurements and advertisement calls; compared with co-occurring P. laticeps it is smaller, with longer dorsal ridges more often present. These characters overlap among individuals. The original 2026 diagnosis, measurements and call comparisons should be used together rather than interpreting color alone as diagnostic. The Mindanao Variable Forest Frog is recognized from Mindanao, including the Mount Hilong-Hilong area of Agusan del Norte. Some older regional records were published under the broader name Platymantis dorsalis (Pitogo et al., 2026; Frost, 2026). The Mindanao Variable Forest Frog has been recorded on the forest floor of mature forest on Mount Hilong-hilong (Frost, 2026). Platymantis habagatan was described in 2026 from the southern Philippine forest-frog complex using comparative morphology, advertisement calls and genetic evidence. Earlier regional literature included these frogs under the broader P. dorsalis name (Pitogo et al., 2026).

In the 2026 redescription, this small to moderate ground-dwelling frog has a broad head, unexpanded terminal discs, prominent subarticular tubercles, a rugose back with scattered raised tubercles and as many as ten irregular dorsal ridges, and barred limbs. The examined specimens measured 23.3–39.8 mm in snout–vent length (mean 29.5 mm), overlapping substantially with P. habagatan. Its most useful reported comparative feature is its advertisement call: a long, gradually intensifying bout lasting about 60–65 seconds, composed of rapidly delivered, short clicking notes (approximately eight notes per second). Its sister species P. habagatan has markedly different call pacing and average body proportions; P. laticeps gives shorter, distinctly pulsed calls. These diagnostic comparisons do not justify labeling an unvouchered individual from mainland Mindanao as P. jagorii because the authors treat its occurrence there as possible rather than securely confirmed. Jagor’s Variable Forest Frog is documented from Samar, Leyte, Bohol and Siargao. Northeastern Mindanao has also been suggested as a possible occurrence, but remains unconfirmed (Pitogo et al., 2026; Frost, 2026). Jagor’s Variable Forest Frog is associated with terrestrial forest habitats in the southern Philippines. It was formerly confused with populations identified as P. dorsalis, so historical records under that name are not necessarily attributable to this species (Pitogo et al., 2026). A 2026 revision reinstated Platymantis jagorii as a distinct species within the southern Philippine forest-frog complex, drawing on morphology, advertisement calls and molecular data (Pitogo et al., 2026).

A relatively large, broad-headed terrestrial forest frog with rough, strongly tuberculate dorsal skin, unexpanded finger and toe tips, prominent subarticular tubercles and no long longitudinal dorsal ridges in the 2026 diagnosis. Reported adult snout–vent lengths are 34.5–45.1 mm in males (mean 39.4 mm) and 42.1–51.8 mm in females (mean 47.1 mm). The back is generally dull brown to dark brown, sometimes with lighter spots; the limbs have transverse bars. In sympatric comparisons, P. laticeps generally exceeds P. habagatan in size and head proportions and has a smaller relative tympanum. The advertisement call comprises brief bouts, approximately 2–6 seconds, with short two- to three-pulsed frequency-modulated notes, unlike the prolonged rapid notes of P. jagorii. Identification requires a combination of morphology and calling characteristics, not size or dorsal color alone. The Broad-headed Variable Forest Frog is documented in northeastern Mindanao, including the Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Balatukan, Mount Lumot and Mount Magdiwata landscapes of Caraga and Northern Mindanao (Pitogo et al., 2026; Frost, 2026). The Broad-headed Variable Forest Frog inhabits terrestrial forest habitats in northeastern Mindanao. Its recognition from formerly broad P. dorsalis identifications affects the interpretation of older habitat records (Pitogo et al., 2026). Platymantis laticeps was reinstated in the 2026 revision of southern Philippine forest frogs formerly classified within P. dorsalis. The study distinguished it using morphology, calls and genetic data (Pitogo et al., 2026).

A small cloud frog with a smooth, finely granular dorsum that may show iridescent emerald-green, orange or creamy-yellow coloration. Its digits have moderately expanded tips but lack interdigital webbing. Male advertisement calls consist of a series of roughly 10–16 short chirping notes (Diesmos et al., 2020). The Navjot Sodhi's Cloud Frog has been documented on Leyte and Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Frost, 2026). Navjot Sodhi’s Cloud Frog inhabits montane forest on Leyte and has also been recorded from northern Leyte and north-central Samar (Diesmos et al., 2020; Frost, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Notable identification characters include a relatively large body and broadly expanded terminal finger discs (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Rabor's Horned Tree Frog is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, and Leyte, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026; Diesmos et al., 2026; Sanguila et al., 2016; AMNH, n.d.). Rabor’s Horned Tree Frog calls from the forest canopy and has been recorded on vegetation in the Taguibo Watershed of Mindanao (Sanguila et al., 2016; Sanguila et al., 2021). This frog gives slowly repeated, pulsed calls, often from high in the forest canopy (Sanguila et al., 2016). Compiled profiles describe activity on the ground and in vegetation, with direct development rather than a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Hijo Forest account describes dark markings on the upper surfaces of both forelimbs and hindlimbs and skin folds that are not arranged in regular parallel series; the features are part of a multi-character identification (Gamalo et al., 2023). The Asian Mangrove Frog has been documented on Mindanao, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Asian Mangrove Frog has been recorded in ground-level and aquatic habitats on northeastern Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). At Hijo Forest, these frogs were frequently found in water, particularly during wet weather (Gamalo et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles also describe aquatic habitat use and larval development (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This frog has an olive-grey back, sometimes marked by a pale vertebral stripe, and yellow bars on the inner hind limbs or groin. In the 2026 comparison with F. moodiei, examined F. vittigera lacked the outer tarsal or fifth-toe flap. AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 80.6 mm (Sanguila et al., 2026; Oliveira et al., 2017). The Philippine Field Frog is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Cabadbaran–Santiago forest, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Agad-Agad, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022). Philippine accounts report this frog from low-elevation ponds, flooded rice fields and irrigation channels, including still pools beside streams at Agusan Marsh. In the Taguibo Watershed analysis, sampled animals occupied aquatic habitats; northeastern Leyte inventories recorded both terrestrial and aquatic observations. At Hijo Forest, survey teams encountered the species frequently in swampy portions of the forest patch (American Museum of Natural History, n.d.; Sanguila et al., 2026; Sanguila et al., 2021; Decena et al., 2023; Gamalo et al., 2023). In northeastern Leyte, observers described loud, honking breeding calls and choruses that formed during or shortly after heavy rain (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: In the Asian bullfrog complex this is a robust, heavily wrinkled species with prominent dorsal ridges, dark blotches and extensively webbed hind feet; identification in Philippine invaded habitats must also consider similarly named historic H. rugulosus records and the currently accepted species concept (Frost, 2026). The East Asian Bullfrog has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The East Asian Bullfrog is associated with cultivated areas. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Specimens discussed from Mt. Kitanglad had a stocky body, short limbs, pale-tipped dorsolateral tubercles, and narrow light bars across the lower jaw (Beukema, 2011). The White-spined Fanged Frog has records from Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Lumot, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; Beukema, 2011; Sanguila et al., 2021). The species has been reported from higher-elevation riparian forest in Mindanao, including mountain streams above 900 m (Frost, 2026). The Taguibo analysis assigned historical Limnonectes diuatus records to aquatic habitats (Sanguila et al., 2021). Two individuals were observed by day beneath leaf litter and rocks in a steep rocky stream at the lower Mt. Kitanglad study site (Beukema, 2011). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and aquatic, with larval development (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: This small fanged frog has interrupted dorsolateral folds, elongated dorsal ridges and incomplete toe webbing. The lower Mount Kitanglad comparison also notes relatively long hind limbs and narrower toe webbing than in L. magnus. AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 49.6 mm (Plaza et al., 2025; Beukema, 2011; Oliveira et al., 2017). The Philippine Swamp Frog has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Supsup et al., 2017). At Tinuy-an Falls, this species was found on fallen logs, the forest floor, and stream margins. Taguibo Watershed records included terrestrial and vegetation and trees, while a northeastern Leyte inventory described observations in aquatic habitats (Plaza et al., 2025; Sanguila et al., 2021; Decena et al., 2023). At two lower Mount Kitanglad sites, frogs of several life stages were found under rocks by day, and night activity was noted at one site (Beukema, 2011). In the Hijo Forest survey, L. leytensis was the most frequently encountered frog species (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The revised fanged-frog complex is differentiated using comparative characters and geographic locality (Abraham et al., 2021). The Tinuy-an account describes a large frog with a conspicuous tympanum, rounded snout and fully webbed feet (Plaza et al., 2025). The Mindanao Fanged Frog has records across Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat and Siargao. Mindanao localities include the Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Balatukan, Mount Lumot, Mount Hamiguitan and Mount Malindang ranges, as well as the Pasonanca area of the Zamboanga Peninsula. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Mount Huraw; on Bohol, Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Supsup et al., 2017; Nuñeza et al., 2010; Diesmos et al., 2026). A 2025 anuran survey along Miral River in Bansalan, Davao del Sur, reports the species in a six-species field assemblage (Ubat, 2025). Field studies document stream and river-associated encounters across eastern and western Mindanao (AMNH, n.d.). The Taguibo Watershed study reported this frog from ground, arboreal and aquatic habitats, drawing on both historical and recent records (Sanguila et al., 2021). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in terrestrial and aquatic habitats (Decena et al., 2023). Stomach-content and stable-isotope analyses in a northeast Mindanao stream study supported generalist feeding on locally available invertebrate prey in the sampled Limnonectes magnus (Plaza et al., 2021). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and aquatic, with larval development. The same compilation lists arthropods in its diet (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 30 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Abungabung Wart Frog was originally described from Abungabung on Basilan under the name Rana micrixalus. The current Amphibian Species of the World account lists both Basilan and mainland Mindanao, whereas Evans and colleagues (2003) treated it as restricted to Basilan. Its mainland occurrence therefore needs a traceable specimen-level reassessment before specific Mindanao localities are accepted (Evans et al., 2003; Frost, 2026). Compiled ecological information describes the Western Mindanao Fanged Frog as using terrestrial and aquatic environments and having a larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A male observed in Pasonanca Natural Park measured 30 mm snout–vent length and had smooth dorsal skin, a smooth supratympanic fold, first and second fingers of equal length, and an inverted V-shaped scapular mark (Lama & Senarillos, 2023). The Philippine Guardian Frog has been documented on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Sinaka, Zamboanga del Norte, and Sarangani (GBIF.org, 2026). Records from Mindanao include secondary-growth and nursery forests with retained vegetation cover (Sanguila et al., 2016). Reported around streams in undisturbed lowland and lower montane forests of Mindanao (Frost, 2026). A male carrying tadpoles on its back was observed in Zamboanga (Lama & Senarillos, 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe activity both on land and in water, with a larval developmental stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 94.2 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Visayan Fanged Frog has records from Leyte and Bohol. On Leyte, records include Mount Pangasugan and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Compiled traits describe the Visayan Fanged Frog as nocturnal and associated with both terrestrial and aquatic environments, with larval development (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Tiny Puddle Frog is represented in a recent comparative diagnosis by very small adults, with a snout–vent length of about 18.0 mm in males and 26.4 mm in females in the cited historical material. The tongue is slightly notched behind and the lower jaw has a single tooth-like projection near its tip (Ninh et al., 2026, comparing Taylor, 1922). The Tiny Puddle Frog has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area, Zamboanga del Norte, and Zamboanga del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026; Frost, 2026). Compiled ecological information places the Tiny Puddle Frog in terrestrial and aquatic environments, with a larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 48 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Common Puddle Frog has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Cabadbaran–Santiago forest, Mount Balatukan, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Lumot, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park, Mount Huraw, and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Common Puddle Frog has been recorded in aquatic habitats on northeastern Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). A northeastern Mindanao stream-food-web study characterized the species as an opportunistic generalist predator on locally available insects, using stomach contents and stable isotope analysis (Plaza et al., 2021). At northeastern Leyte sites, frogs sat immersed in narrow shallow streams or isolated pools and sometimes sheltered beneath deep leaf litter by day (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as fossorial and aquatic, with larval development. The same compilation lists arthropods in its diet, both diurnal and nocturnal activity and offspring counts of 107–140 (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A small brown to grayish-brown frog with variable mottling and sometimes paired dorsolateral lines, measuring roughly 12–30 mm in body length (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). The Greenhouse Frog is recorded on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Agad-Agad, Agusan del Norte, and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022). Direct development occurs within terrestrial eggs, with small froglets hatching without an aquatic tadpole stage (Animal Diversity Web, n.d.). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial, aquatic and arboreal, and indicate direct development without a free-living larval stage. The same compilation lists arthropods in its diet, nocturnal activity, and offspring counts of 2–26 (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The museum account cites recent field habitat work in the Mount Gutom and Agusan regions (AMNH, n.d.). AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 65.1 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Mindanao Litter Frog is reported from Mindanao, Basilan and Samar. Dinagat is listed in the 2025 national amphibian checklist but is not included in the specialist distribution account, leaving that island attribution unresolved (Frost, 2026; Diesmos et al., 2026). The 2016 northeast Mindanao surveys encountered this frog at agricultural edges beside second-growth vegetation, tree nurseries and lowland forest riparian sites (Sanguila et al., 2016). Sanguila and colleagues reported specimens on the mountains Magdiwata, Hilong-hilong, Balatukan and Lumot at elevations reaching 1,500 m (Sanguila et al., 2016). Recent voucher-supported records in the Taguibo Watershed were assigned to ground-level habitats within riparian and terrestrial survey zones (Sanguila et al., 2021). AmphiBIO summarizes published ecological traits as habitat categories: terrestrial (Oliveira et al., 2017). Earlier authors confused these Philippine litter frogs with Leptobrachium hasseltii before formal description (AMNH, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A medium-sized, broad-headed frog with paired horn-like upper eyelids, prominent dorsolateral folds, relatively slender legs and short toe webbing (Plaza et al., 2025). The Mindanao Horned Frog has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Frost, 2026). Documented habitats range from disturbed to intact montane forests. Individuals have been encountered among leaf litter and on the forest floor, including beside streams and trails (Plaza et al., 2025). A specimen identified under the historical name Megophrys stejnegeri was documented beside cultivated land along a forest edge at about 700 m on Mt. Hilong-hilong (Sanguila et al., 2016). A Taguibo Watershed inventory listed specimens under the earlier combination Megophrys stejnegeri and recorded ground-substrate use in sampled riparian and terrestrial zones. The publication’s source name is retained here for traceability (Sanguila et al., 2021). The northeastern Leyte inventory, using the former combination Megophrys stejnegeri, reports male calls from stream banks and forest interiors during or after heavy rain (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: The original description, published as Oreophryne nana from Camiguin Island, is based on a small frog whose adult female type series measured 17–20 mm in snout–vent length (no mature males were available). Brown and Alcala (1967) described a head broader than long, a short blunt snout, moderately expanded terminal discs on fingers and toes except the first finger, no webbing, dark mottling on the venter, and no subarticular tubercles on the hands. The third-finger and third-toe discs were approximately equal in size. These measurements and characters apply to the original Camiguin specimens, rather than an established range-wide population. The absence of hand tubercles was initially used to distinguish it from O. anulata, but Sanguila et al. (2016) found that the degree of hand-tubercle development varies among frogs on mainland Mindanao. Those mainland animals were reported as Oreophryne cf. nana, not securely assigned to A. nana. The accepted species is currently confirmed from Camiguin Island, outside the Greater Mindanao PAIC; matching a single superficial character does not establish a new mainland record. The Camiguin Cross Frog is currently known from Camiguin Island, outside the Greater Mindanao PAIC. Older records from Mindanao, Samar and Leyte under the name Oreophryne nana remain unresolved under the current species concept (Frost, 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Camiguin Cross Frog is known from the Mount Hibok-Hibok area of Camiguin, outside Greater Mindanao PAIC. Related frogs recorded on Mindanao are not securely assigned to this species (Frost, 2026). The name Aphantophryne nana is based on the Camiguin Island type series. Some Mindanao frogs have been reported under the tentative identification Oreophryne cf. nana (Frost, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Mt. Kitanglad specimens were dark brown to black with pale body reticulations, strongest on the underside, and dermal projections at the elbows and heels (Beukema, 2011). The Saffron-bellied Frog has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Mount Sinaka, and Davao del Sur. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011; GIZ, 2013; Sanguila et al., 2016; Nuñeza et al., 2010). Two individuals were found in leaf litter on the forest floor beside a small stream at a lower Mt. Kitanglad site (Beukema, 2011). Two individuals were encountered by day in leaf litter on the forest floor beside a small stream in the lower Mt. Kitanglad Range (Beukema, 2011). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and aquatic, with larval development. The same compilation lists arthropods in its diet (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The Agusan Marsh treatment describes a dark X-shaped marking on the back and a pair of dark round spots near the groin. The underside is tan to pink, with scattered darker markings (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Sticky Frog has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Supsup et al., 2017). The Philippine Sticky Frog has been observed near temporary pools and water-filled cavities by streams, including calling and gravid individuals. It releases a sticky skin secretion when disturbed (Sanguila et al., 2021; Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 47 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Philippine Narrowmouth Toad has regional records from Mindanao, Dinagat and Leyte, including reports from the Andanan Watershed and Agusan Marsh on Mindanao. The recent Philippine checklist assigns populations on Mindanao, Siargao and Bucas Grande to Kaloula conjuncta meridionalis, but lists Camiguin Sur as well, an island outside the PAIC scope of this volume. The specific Dinagat and Leyte observations should be rechecked under this subspecies treatment before their identities are stated as verified (GBIF.org, 2026; EYS, 2025). The Philippine Narrowmouth Toad forms breeding aggregations at the start of the rainy season in Mindanao. Compiled traits describe arboreal habitat use and an arthropod diet (Sanguila et al., 2016; Oliveira et al., 2017).

records.p: The taxonomic catalog describes an endemic narrow-mouthed frog recorded at low elevations across multiple Philippine islands, including Luzon, Samar and Mindanao (American Museum of Natural History, n.d.). Specimens assigned to Kaloula picta in the 2026 Agusan Marsh account have an olive-brown dorsum with a large, variable dark medial marking, pale-brown to pinkish-tan underside, and webbed toes with little to no expansion of terminal discs (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Painted Narrowmouth Toad has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Taguibo Watershed, Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Sanguila et al., 2026). A Caraga amphibian field survey recorded Kaloula picta beside streams and near cornfields outside the selected mining site near Bunawan, Agusan del Sur (Galolo et al., 2021). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in vegetation and trees (Sanguila et al., 2021). Reported breeding gatherings occur in rice fields and temporary rain pools (Sanguila et al., 2016). Only two individuals were recorded in the northeastern Leyte study, both in disturbed pasture-associated aquatic or ground-level habitats (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as fossorial and terrestrial, with larval development. The same compilation lists arthropods in its diet (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The Asiatic Painted Narrowmouth Toad is a stout, short-limbed microhylid with a small head and rounded body. Its grey or brown back bears broad, dark-edged yellowish to orange bands along the sides, and the fingertips and toe tips are blunt and somewhat expanded (National Parks Board Singapore Flora & Fauna Web, n.d.; Sanguila et al., 2026). The Asiatic Painted Narrowmouth Toad has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Agad-Agad, Davao del Norte, and Lanao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022). The species is frequently recorded in disturbed or developed settings, where calls are often heard around heavy rain. At Agusan Marsh, specimens were collected in farmland adjoining peat and freshwater swamps (National Parks Board Singapore Flora & Fauna Web, n.d.; Sanguila et al., 2026). Calling is commonly associated with heavy rainfall. Published trait compilations list nocturnal activity and a mainly arthropod diet (National Parks Board Singapore Flora & Fauna Web, n.d.; Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: This stocky frog has variable brown coloring, a mottled underside and expanded digital tips (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Mindanao Cross Frog has records from Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Apo, and Zamboanga del Norte. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013; Sanguila et al., 2026). Agusan Marsh calling records included frogs on floating wetland vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2026). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and arboreal, and indicate direct development without a free-living larval stage. The same compilation lists arthropods in its diet and offspring counts of 3–9 (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 75 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Green Paddy Frog has been documented on Samar and Leyte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park, Mount Huraw, and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Green Paddy Frog has been recorded in aquatic habitats on northeastern Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe use of both terrestrial and aquatic habitats and a larval developmental stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 67 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Mindanao Striped Stream Frog has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Males assigned to Pulchrana grandocula called around stream pools at reduced flow (Sanguila et al., 2016). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and aquatic, with larval development. The same compilation lists arthropods in its diet (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The original Mount Busa description emphasizes expanded digital discs, strong lateral pigmentation and characters distinguishing this frog from Hylarana grandocula (Frost, 2026). The Guttman's Stream Frog has been documented on Mindanao, including Busa Mountain Range and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The regional checklist associates Guttman’s Stream Frog with forests and streams. Current specialist taxonomy places confirmed populations in elevated parts of the Mount Parker–Busa region of southern Mindanao, rather than throughout all the island’s streams. The reported habitat association is therefore geographically limited (Frost, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The species has an elongated pointed snout, bronze-brown back, white upper-lip markings and humeral glands (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Nicobar Frog has been documented from Agusan Marsh in Agusan del Sur, northeastern Mindanao. These records provide regional occurrence evidence beyond the islands previously listed in the older national checklist (Sanguila et al., 2026; EYS, 2025). An Agusan Marsh herpetological study reported animals calling in wetland vegetation, including individuals associated with floating plant mats. These observations document calling microhabitats at the surveyed marsh sites and do not establish habitat selection across the taxon’s regional range (Sanguila et al., 2026).

records.p: A comparatively large, slender stream frog with well-developed digital discs and flanks that grade from darker above to lighter below. Enlarged infracloacal tubercles occur in most examined individuals, unlike the condition reported for S. acai. Historical identification of frogs in the S. everetti complex requires attention to geographic and taxonomic revisions (Brown et al., 2017). Under the revision of Brown et al. (2017), Sanguirana everetti is associated with western and southern Mindanao. Earlier records assigned to this name from northeastern Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte require reassessment because the eastern lineage is now recognized as S. mearnsi. The unrevised GBIF records should not be interpreted as confirmed S. everetti occurrences (Brown et al., 2017). The Mindanao Torrent Frog is associated with forests and waterways. The species was described from the Zamboanga region on Mindanao, with a long taxonomic history under Rana and other combinations (AMNH, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Expanded finger and toe disks and distinct white glandular areas near the vent aid identification (Plaza et al., 2025). The northeastern Leyte species account describes a metallic bright-green dorsum, bright-yellow dorsolateral folds, and an absence of transverse tibial bars (Decena et al., 2023). The northeastern Leyte field account identifies a bright metallic-green back, contrasting yellow dorsolateral folds and an absence of transverse bars on the tibia as notable external characters (Decena et al., 2023). The Mearn's Stream Frog has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Lumot, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mearn's Stream Frog has been observed in streamside vegetation at Tinuy-an Falls (Plaza et al., 2025). Both historical and recent Taguibo Watershed specimen records contributed to an analysis that found use of ground, arboreal and aquatic habitats by Sanguirana mearnsi (Sanguila et al., 2021). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in aquatic habitats (Decena et al., 2023). Four frogs were observed on rocks and logs beside streams surrounded by coconut plantations in the sampled Leyte Cordillera locality (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 51.3 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Mindanao Rock Frog has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Basilan, including Cabadbaran–Santiago forest on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026; Sanguila et al., 2016). At Pamugtoan River in Mount Hamiguitan, individuals were observed on riparian shrubs and ferns beside a boulder-strewn stream in disturbed lower montane forest at 650 m elevation (Maglangit et al., 2020). Field observers found individuals in leaf axils of ferns and shrubs immediately beside mountain streams (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Taguibo Watershed inventory documented historical and recent specimens; the study’s habitat analysis reported ground, arboreal and aquatic microhabitat use at the surveyed sites (Sanguila et al., 2021). A Mount Hamiguitan survey recorded leech parasitism in 12 of 31 observed frogs, documenting an interaction in a riverine population (Maglangit et al., 2020). Observers in the northeastern Leyte inventory found the frog on streamside rocks and boulders and perched in overhanging vegetation beside flowing water (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial, aquatic and arboreal, with larval development (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A treefrog with fringed skin projections along the limbs and outer margins of the feet, and a cream to yellow underside; dorsal color ranges from brown to gray (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Frilled Tree Frog has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013; Sanguila et al., 2016). Agusan Marsh researchers observed individuals in forest near open river systems within freshwater swamp habitats (Sanguila et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The historical description portrays a frog with a rounded snout, moderate digital discs, partly webbed fingers and almost fully webbed toes. It has violet-brown upperparts with irregular darker spots and crossbars, banded limbs, and a conspicuous pale spot below the eye followed by a smaller spot (Boulenger, 1882). The White-spotted Gliding Frog has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Cabadbaran–Santiago forest, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, and Surigao del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023; Tirona et al., 2026). The Hijo Forest account summarizes earlier observations of the flying frog on understorey vegetation and rocks near rivers or swamps; at Hijo itself the species appeared in the 2010 historical assessment but was not redetected in the recent fieldwork (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: Its orange-to-cinnamon back is covered in white-tipped projections; the underside is also bright orange (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Mindanao Spiny Tree Frog has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Sanguila et al., 2026; Nuñeza et al., 2010). In the Leyte Cordillera and Babatngon ranges, the species was encountered in vegetation and trees (Decena et al., 2023). One individual was seen at night on a plant about 0.5 m above ground in montane forest on Mt. Aminduen (796 m elevation); it was found outside the standardized strip plot (Decena et al., 2023). Calling individuals have been observed in tree cavities, producing soft, chirping whistles (Sanguila et al., 2016). Compiled ecological profiles describe ground-level and arboreal habitat use and larval development (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Males have an acutely pointed snout and a sharply angled canthal ridge; the gray or brown back is variable but lacks a distinct dark cross-shaped marking (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Pointed-Snouted Shrub Frog has records from Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Malindang Range, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Magdiwata, and Surigao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Tirona et al., 2026; Nuñeza et al., 2010). After rain, calling males perch beneath leaves roughly 0.3–1 m above the forest floor, giving decelerating, rattle-like calls (Sanguila et al., 2016). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and arboreal, and indicate direct development without a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The shrub frog has a broad head, pointed snout, large digital disks and webbed toes (Plaza et al., 2025). The Mt. Kitanglad account describes an obtusely pointed snout, unwebbed fingers, webbed toes, a weakly distinct tympanum, and a coarsely granular abdomen (Beukema, 2011). The Leyte Shrub Frog has records from Leyte, Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011). The Leyte Shrub Frog has been recorded in vegetation and trees at Tinuy-an Falls (Plaza et al., 2025). At Tinuy-an Falls, individuals perched on understory leaves less than half a meter above ground (Plaza et al., 2025). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in vegetation and trees (Decena et al., 2023). Two individuals were found concealed in leaf litter beside a small brook at the lower Mt. Kitanglad study site (Beukema, 2011). At northeastern Leyte sites, calling males perched on leaves of understory plants approximately 0.3–1 m above ground. The study also describes occasional concealment among ferns and moss (Decena et al., 2023). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and arboreal, and indicate direct development without a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: Reports describe a variable brown or dark-spotted upper surface and banded hind limbs in frogs from northeastern Mindanao (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Mottled Shrub Frog has records from Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Dulang-dulang, Mount Lumot, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The AmphiBIO trait compilation codes the species as terrestrial and arboreal, with direct development rather than a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 35.4 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Rufous Shrub Frog is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Lumot, and Misamis Occidental (GBIF.org, 2026; Nuñeza et al., 2010). Reported from forested mountain habitats at approximately 800–2,300 m in the Mount Malindang region of Mindanao (Frost, 2026). Surveys in northeastern Mindanao associate this frog with upper montane forest (Sanguila et al., 2016). Compiled traits indicate direct development without a free-living aquatic larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 44 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Worcester's Shrub Frog has been documented on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Apo, Mount Lumot, and Zamboanga del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Frost, 2026; Nuñeza et al., 2010). The reported advertisement call is a loud, short crunch-like note, often repeated two or three times; surveys recorded calling frogs in vegetation along forest edges and disturbed mountain habitats (Sanguila et al., 2016). Compiled ecological profiles describe the species as terrestrial and arboreal, and indicate direct development without a free-living larval stage (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

This relatively slender, long-legged tree frog may be brown, grey or yellowish above, sometimes with four narrow longitudinal dark stripes. Its fingers and toes end in expanded, flattened pads that aid climbing. AmphiBIO lists a compiled body-size value of 80 mm (National Parks Board Singapore Flora & Fauna Web, n.d.; Oliveira et al., 2017). The Common Southeast Asian Tree Frog has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023; Tirona et al., 2026; Sanguila et al., 2016). This nocturnal tree frog uses shrubs, trees and other vegetation in forests, settlements and disturbed landscapes (National Parks Board Singapore Flora & Fauna Web, n.d.). The species feeds on insects and is active chiefly at night. At Agusan Marsh, calling frogs were found among floating plants, at grassy pool margins and on overhanging branches (National Parks Board Singapore Flora & Fauna Web, n.d.; Sanguila et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 70 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Emerald Gliding Frog is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, and Leyte, including Mount Malindang Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013; Sanguila et al., 2016). The AmphiBIO trait compilation codes the species as terrestrial and arboreal, with larval development (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 250 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Basilan Caecilian is recorded on Mindanao and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area (GBIF.org, 2026; Frost, 2026). The AmphiBIO trait compilation codes the species as fossorial, terrestrial and aquatic (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

AmphiBIO gives a compiled body-size value of 323 mm (Oliveira et al., 2017). The Mindanao Caecilian has been documented on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026; Frost, 2026). A Philippine caecilian status review reports 20 collected individuals, many sheltering beneath rocks, decomposing logs or other debris in shallow pools or dry streambeds. Examined voucher stomachs contained ants, water beetles and other arthropods. These are study observations rather than a quantified dietary preference (Diesmos, 2012). AmphiBIO summarizes published ecological traits as habitat categories: fossorial, terrestrial, aquatic (Oliveira et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: The Philippine Crocodile is a comparatively small freshwater crocodile with a broad head, prominent dorsal armour and a strong tail. Its dark-brown upperparts bear darker transverse bars above a paler underside. Enlarged postoccipital and nuchal scales help distinguish it from the Saltwater Crocodile; a comparative study recorded about 22–25 ventral scale rows and 4–6 enlarged postoccipital scales in examined Philippine Crocodiles (DENR Protected Areas and Wildlife Bureau / Royal Melbourne, 2005; Ross & Alcala, 1983, as reviewed in later crocodile literature). The Philippine Crocodile is documented in central Mindanao, including Ligawasan Marsh and the Muleta River system of Bukidnon (IUCN SSC and Secretariat, 2025). The Philippine Crocodile inhabits freshwater rivers, creeks, ponds, lakes and marshes. Published habitat accounts describe both riverine and wetland settings; northern Sierra Madre surveys in Luzon also reported animals in coastal river reaches with saline conditions (DENR Protected Areas and Wildlife Bureau / Royal Melbourne, 2005; Smithsonian National Zoo, n.d.; Brown et al., 2013). Females build mound or hole nests and both sexes may guard them. The Smithsonian account reports clutches of seven to thirty eggs (Smithsonian National Zoo, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: In the comparative scale material examined, Saltwater Crocodiles had approximately 29–34 ventral scale rows and 0–2 enlarged postoccipitals, compared with 22–25 ventral rows and 4–6 enlarged postoccipitals in Philippine Crocodiles. Other morphological characters are also used for identification (Ross & Alcala, 1983, as reviewed in subsequent crocodile literature). The Saltwater Crocodile is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). Saltwater Crocodiles use tidal rivers, estuaries, mangrove swamps and coastal waters, and may also occupy freshwater rivers and lakes well inland. Females build mound nests near suitable water bodies; these broad habitat characteristics do not establish occupancy at a particular Greater Mindanao site (Carpenter & Niem, 2001). The Saltwater Crocodile is an egg-laying species (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: The 2026 revision of Philippine Bronchocela diagnoses this Mindanao lineage by short, lanceolate nuchal spines, a nuchal crest of 9–12 spines separated from the dorsal crest, and narrow, strongly keeled lateral body scales. Its combination of crest and scale characters is more informative than a general green lizard appearance (Supsup et al., 2026). The Philippine Bloodsucker has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hilong-Hilong and Surigao del Norte (Tirona et al., 2026). The Philippine Bloodsucker is associated with forests and shrublands.

The patagia are supported by five elongate ribs and the head bears a black spot on each side (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Two-spotted Flying Lizard has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Huraw on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Supsup et al., 2017). Agusan Marsh records include peat-swamp forest and relatively low perches in regenerating vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2026). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in vegetation and trees (Decena et al., 2023). A single individual at the northeastern Leyte study site was observed on a tree trunk about 4 m above ground by day in riparian vegetation within selectively logged dipterocarp forest (Decena et al., 2023). Females lay eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Mt. Hamiguitan account describes grey dorsal coloration with dark blotches and chartreuse-green patagia edged in dark brown or black in observed individuals (Supsup et al., 2017). The Chartreuse-spotted Flying Lizard is recorded on Mindanao and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Lumot, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; Beukema, 2011). Recent survey records from Taguibo Watershed placed Draco cyanopterus in vegetation and trees of the sampled terrestrial zone (Sanguila et al., 2021). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). At Mt. Hamiguitan, one female was observed burying four eggs in sand along a riverbank, providing a site-specific record of nesting behavior (Supsup et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A photographically identified Mt. Kitanglad individual displayed vivid malachite-green coloration and ultramarine-blue ciliary scales. The lizard was not captured for detailed examination (Beukema, 2011). The Günther's Flying Lizard has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Zamboanga del Sur, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011). The Günther's Flying Lizard is associated with forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A relatively large Philippine Draco with rib-supported gliding membranes. Males show a bright orange dewlap and red ventral patagia, whereas females have dark ventral patagia; body and membrane patterns distinguish it from sympatric flying lizards (Siler, n.d.). The Mindanao Flying Lizard is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Magdiwata, and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park, Mount Huraw, and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Records and species accounts associate this arboreal lizard with primary and mature secondary rainforest (Siler, n.d.). Like other Draco, it glides between trees using laterally extended, rib-supported patagial membranes (Siler, n.d.). This flying lizard lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). In Smith’s 1982 eastern Mindanao field series, a female from primary forest around 650 m elevation carried two oviductal eggs measuring 17.5 and 18.4 mm. Examined stomach contents included insects from several families; neither a clutch-frequency estimate nor a population-level feeding preference follows (Smith, 1993). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The gliding membranes show conspicuous pattern differences between the sexes; females can be more vividly patterned than males (Uetz et al., 2026). The Ornate Flying Lizard has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve and Bukidnon. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in vegetation and trees (Decena et al., 2023). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Four individuals of this flying lizard were seen on a single occasion in coconut-plantation vegetation in the lowlands of the Babatngon Range, Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The taxon historically described as Draco volans reticulatus has a dark ring around the eye, a white chin crossed by a fine network of dark spots, and pale patches at the sides of the nape. The male was described with an enlarged scale above the eye and a nuchal crest of more than 22 scales, while the lateral gliding membrane sometimes shows blue areas (The Reptile Database, 2026, after Musters 1983). The Reticulated Flying Lizard has been documented on Leyte and Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). In the revision’s field observations, Draco reticulatus occurred mainly in open coconut plantations and was observed using well-sunlit trees on Bohol in sympatry with D. bimaculatus and D. ornatus. The species is part of the egg-laying Draco radiation, with oviparity reported for this taxon in the species treatment (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This lizard has a large head, strong hindlimbs, and a neck crest generally separated from the lower dorsal crest. The base of the tail shows alternating pale and dark bands; mature males commonly have blue eyes (Sanguila et al., 2026). Lizards reported as Gonocephalus semperi have been recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte and Bohol. A recent taxonomic reassessment indicates that some older island records may belong to different lineages (Del Prado et al., 2026; recent Gonocephalus revision, 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Anglehead Lizard is broadly associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). In the 1982 eastern Mindanao lizard collection, one female of the taxon then reported as Gonyocephalus semperi contained three developing eggs measuring 5.8, 6.6 and 7.3 mm. The same paper recorded insect and other arthropod remains in examined stomachs. This preserves the historical name and specimen scope (Smith, 1993). An archipelago-wide multilocus analysis recovered 12 putative Philippine Gonocephalus lineages, including differentiated southern island populations. The authors did not assign the available species names, including G. semperi, to individual diagnosable genetic lineages; these findings therefore cannot be converted into a verified island-by-island distribution of G. semperi (Welton et al., 2017). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: The Philippine Sailfin Lizard is a large agamid with a distinctive laterally flattened, serrated dorsal sail extending from the hip region toward the base of the tail. The hind limbs are longer than the forelimbs, and the scales beneath the toes are conspicuously expanded. A juvenile from the Agusan River measured 95 mm snout–vent length (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Sailfin Lizard is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hilong-Hilong on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Sanguila et al., 2021; Maglangit et al., 2022; Gamalo et al., 2023; Diesmos et al., 2026). Recorded on overhanging trees beside streams and riverbanks near Agusan Marsh agricultural land (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Taguibo study associated the sampled sailfin lizards with ground-level habitats in its riparian and terrestrial survey-zone analysis (Sanguila et al., 2021). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in aquatic habitats (Decena et al., 2023). In northeastern Mindanao, sailfin lizards were observed active by day and resting in rock crevices along rivers at night at sampled sites between 170 and 420 m elevation (Sanguila et al., 2016). At Hijo Forest in Tagum City, observers found one lizard on a pandan plant and another crossing a coastal road near beach forest (Gamalo et al., 2023). In northeastern Leyte, individuals were observed sleeping on stream boulders or low shrubs at night and running across water in daylight (Decena et al., 2023). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Green, grey, yellow and brown color forms are documented for this variable vine snake (Uetz et al., 2026). The Asian Vine Snake is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Lumot, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Taguibo Watershed records place this vine snake in trees and other vegetation (Sanguila et al., 2021). Sleeping snakes were seen on low shrubs beside forest edges (Sanguila et al., 2016). A diurnal, fully arboreal snake that gives birth to live young rather than laying external eggs (Uetz et al., 2026).

The Philippine Blunt-headed Cat Snake has a series of roughly forty dark crossbands on the back that broaden toward the sides. The illustrated Philippine snake key also distinguishes it from similar Boiga by nineteen rows of dorsal scales at midbody and a single preocular scale (Weinell et al., 2019). The Philippine Blunt-headed Cat Snake is recorded on Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The species has been characterized as fully arboreal in comparative snake-habitat literature summarized by Uetz et al (2026). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). A multilocus phylogeny placed Boiga angulata in the drapiezii species group alongside B. schultzei and other relatives. This phylogenetic placement provides no diagnostic field characters or Philippine island-level occurrence records by itself (Weinell et al., 2021). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Dog-toothed Cat Snake is distinguished in the illustrated Philippine key by twenty-three dorsal scale rows around midbody and three anterior temporal scales on each side of the head. These scale characters help separate it from similar Philippine Boiga (Weinell et al., 2019). The Dog-toothed Cat Snake has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Agad-Agad, Lanao del Norte, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022; Supsup et al., 2017; Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Leyte Cordillera and Babatngon ranges, the species was encountered in ground-level habitats (Decena et al., 2023). A phylogenetic study compared Boiga cynodon populations from the Philippines, Sundaland and Indochina (Weinell et al., 2021). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The Mindanao subspecies B. d. latifasciata has a black body with pale crossbands and vertical pupils (Plaza et al., 2025). The Mangrove Snake has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Bega Watershed, Agusan del Sur, and Davao Oriental. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017). Climbing and use of aboveground vegetation are documented; a comparative review characterizes this species as partly arboreal (Uetz et al., 2026). An adult was documented swimming through a shallow stream at Tinuy-an Falls (Plaza et al., 2025). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). A multilocus analysis found that sampled members of the Boiga dendrophila complex, including B. d. melanota and B. tanahjampeana, do not form a single evolutionary lineage (Weinell et al., 2021). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Taylor’s diagnosis of this slender cat snake includes an enlarged vertebral scale row and a large preocular reaching the upper head shields, in addition to the two ventral black longitudinal lines described in the baseline (Uetz et al., 2026). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The White-spotted Cat Snake has records from Mindanao (Leviton et al., 2018). The White-spotted Cat Snake is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This small reed snake has pale dorsal scales marked by dark networks and usually an interrupted pale stripe with dark borders along the lowest row of body scales. In the Philippine key, its chin shields contact the mental scale, and it lacks the dark belly bands of C. lumbricoidea (Weinell et al., 2019). The Philippine Reed Snake has records from Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, and Davao del Sur. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011; GIZ, 2013). This species was recorded in soil and beneath forest-floor debris (Sanguila et al., 2016). An egg-laying snake (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The Variable Reed Snake can be distinguished from several other Philippine Calamaria by dark bands across the underside of the body. Its mental scale also meets the front pair of chin shields, a useful feature in the illustrated identification key (Weinell et al., 2019). The Variable Reed Snake is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Mount Lumot, Misamis Oriental, and Bukidnon. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011; Sanguila et al., 2016). In northeastern Leyte, the species was recorded in ground-level habitats (Decena et al., 2023). The snake lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). A single animal was encountered in daylight among leaf litter and riparian boulders within dipterocarp forest in northeastern Leyte. The study also discusses fossorial habits based on prior literature, so this paragraph reports only the directly documented daytime encounter (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).
