records.p: This slender snake has a dark back with reddish-yellow crossbars, a round pupil, and 17 dorsal scale rows at midbody. The outermost dorsal scale row is notched (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Paradise Flying Snake is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Davao del Norte, and Lanao del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). This snake is fully arboreal and uses the tree canopy and branches (Uetz et al., 2026). A tree-dwelling gliding snake, observed resting high in vegetation at night (Sanguila et al., 2016). Its lateral body shape allows controlled gliding between elevated positions; it reproduces by laying eggs (Uetz et al., 2026).

This rat snake has a round pupil and a brown-to-olive body; in the nominate form, the tail is noticeably paler or more reddish than the hindbody. Tail-color contrasts vary among the forms treated in the Philippine key and should be considered alongside other characters (Weinell et al., 2019; Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Red-tailed Ratsnake has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Misamis Occidental, and Lanao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Leyte Cordillera and Babatngon ranges, the species was encountered in aquatic habitats (Decena et al., 2023). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

A dark stripe extends behind the eye toward the neck, and a narrow pale stripe runs along the lower flanks; total length can reach about 131 cm (Uetz et al., 2026). This slender bronzeback has a broad dark postocular stripe extending onto the neck, a pale ventrolateral line and a particularly long tail comprising roughly one third of total length (Uetz et al., 2026). The Maren's Bronzeback Snake has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Taguibo Watershed, Agusan del Sur, and Davao Oriental. On Leyte, records include Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; GIZ, 2013). Tree-dwelling specimens were recorded from the Agusan region (Sanguila et al., 2016). Two catalogued recent specimens from Taguibo Watershed (MBS 475 and MBS 481) were assigned to vegetation and trees in the field-record analysis (Sanguila et al., 2021). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Described as an active daytime snake that forages and moves among trees (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

Its midbody has thirteen dorsal scale rows, with dark longitudinal flank stripes and a pale lower-side stripe (Sanguila et al., 2026). Midbody dorsal scales number thirteen rows in examined specimens (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Philippine Bronzeback Snake has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Agad-Agad, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Maglangit et al., 2022). The Philippine Bronzeback Snake is associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine Whip Snake is a slender, long-tailed snake that differs from the related D. rubescens in lacking the loreal scale between the nasal region and the eye. The illustrated key also reports fewer ventral scales in D. philippina, although the ranges approach one another (Weinell et al., 2019). The Philippine Whip Snake is recorded on Leyte and Mindanao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Whip Snake is associated with forests. The original type locality of Dryophiops philippina is on northern Luzon. The Reptile Database documents its historical nomenclature and geographic records (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

A long, slender tree snake usually green or yellow-green over the body, with a tail that may be reddish, brown or gray. It has smooth dorsal scales; head-scale proportions and scale-row counts distinguish it from related Gonyosoma and allied genera. Tail color alone is variable and should not be used as the sole diagnostic feature (Wallach et al., 2024). The Red-tailed Green Ratsnake is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Zamboanga del Sur, and Davao Oriental. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; Sanguila et al., 2016; Gamalo et al., 2023). Published behavior records describe a primarily tree-dwelling snake, active during daylight and using forest vegetation (Uetz et al., 2026). This rat snake lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). In the Hijo inventory, this species was reported by site management but was neither documented in the authors’ recent fieldwork nor in the cited 2010 survey. The evidence is a local report, not a direct encounter (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

A slender, mostly brown or purplish-brown wolf snake with fine pale reticulations or broken light markings, sometimes accompanied by a pale collar behind the head. The pattern may be faint, so identification should not rest on color alone (Lanza, 1999). The Common Wolf Snake is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Bato, Misamis Occidental, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Common Wolf Snake has been recorded near residences and other heavily modified lowland sites (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Common Wolf Snake reproduces by laying eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: Ferron’s Wolf Snake has dark rings that encircle both the body and tail, unlike the incomplete dark bands of the similar L. dumerili. The illustrated key also notes approximately ten upper labial scales, of which the fourth through sixth border the eye (Weinell et al., 2019). Ferron’s Wolf Snake is documented on Samar. A separate Southern Leyte identification appears in a Mount Nacolod survey, but the specialist and national range summaries do not yet establish that island occurrence (GIZ, 2013; Uetz et al., 2026). The Ferron's Wolf Snake is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Spotted Short-headed Snake has distinct dark blotches along the back that extend down to the ventral scales. It usually has two preocular scales, a combination used to separate it from the related O. ancorus in the illustrated Philippine key (Weinell et al., 2019). The Spotted Short-headed Snake has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Agusan del Norte, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017; The Reptile Database, n.d.; Sanguila et al., 2016). The Spotted Short-headed Snake is broadly associated with forests and habitats along rivers and streams. The species lays eggs (The Reptile Database, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The Barred Short-headed Snake has a pale stripe along the vertebral line and conspicuous rectangular black markings on the belly, without the prominent dorsal blotches of some related kukri snakes. The illustrated key also reports fifteen dorsal scale rows at midbody (Weinell et al., 2019). The Barred Short-headed Snake was listed from Southern Leyte in a Mount Nacolod survey. That locality is absent from the 2026 Philippine reptile checklist and specialist distribution summaries, so the identification remains unconfirmed (GIZ, 2013; Uetz et al., 2026). The Barred Short-headed Snake is associated with forests. This kukri snake lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: A stream-associated snake with a slender body, distinguished by its head-scale arrangement (Uetz et al., 2026). The Alcala's Mountain Keelback Snake has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area (GBIF.org, 2026). A stream-associated aquatic snake recorded in flowing water rather than an exclusively terrestrial setting (Uetz et al., 2026). The species is nocturnal. Reported prey include small fish, frogs and tadpoles, freshwater shrimp and earthworms; reproduction is oviparous (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.b: ◆ Philippine endemic     •     ◉ IUCN DD     •     ✦ Exceptionally rare
records.p: Diagnostic scalation includes absence of loreal, preocular and supraocular scales; the frontal scale reaches the margin of the eye (Uetz et al., 2026). Leviton and Brown’s published diagnosis, reproduced by the Reptile Database, records 12 maxillary teeth, an internasal contacting the upper labials, and a postocular fused to the ocular shield. These characters supplement the stated absence of several orbital shields and derive from the historical taxonomic treatment (Uetz et al., 2026). The Zamboanga Burrowing snake has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Zamboanga Burrowing snake is associated with forests. The broad classification does not establish soil, litter, or other retreat sites at named Greater Mindanao localities. Egg laying is recorded for this species (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

This small Philippine snake lacks a loreal scale, and its prefrontal reaches the upper lip scales. In the illustrated Philippine key, the parietal touches both the fourth and fifth supralabials. Scales along the lowest dorsal row have dark centers and pale edges, and the brown ventral scales have paler rear margins. These characters separate it from the similar Pseudorabdion montanum in the cited key (Weinell et al., 2019). Günther’s Dwarf Reed Snake is recorded from Mindanao, alongside other Philippine islands (Uetz et al., 2026). The Visayan Light-scaled Burrowing Snake is broadly associated with forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). The historical combinations Typhlogeophis brevis and Oxycalamus oxycephalus are part of this snake’s synonymy history. A cited older name may reflect a different identification standard, so historical localities require checking against the original specimens and current diagnostic criteria (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

records.p: The described head scalation includes a loreal scale but lacks a separate preocular, with seven maxillary teeth reported (Uetz et al., 2026). The historical diagnosis reported more than 30 subcaudals, anterior chin shields touching the mental, and seven maxillary teeth, based on three examined specimens. The Reptile Database lists holotype MCZ 25749 from Saub, Cotabato, Mindanao; these are type-series characters, not population-wide frequencies (Uetz et al., 2026). The Taylor's Burrowing Snake has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Taylor's Burrowing Snake is broadly associated with forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine Smooth-scaled Mountain Ratsnake has smooth scales along the middle of the back and fourteen longitudinal dorsal scale rows on the front third of the body. This distinguishes it from the similar P. carinata, which has keeled middorsal scales and more scale rows there (Weinell et al., 2019). The Philippine Smooth-scaled Mountain Ratsnake has been documented on Leyte, including Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Smooth-scaled Mountain Ratsnake is associated with forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

An ear-like whitish spot behind the eye is reflected in the species name and is useful as a head-pattern character (Uetz et al., 2026). The White-lined Water Snake is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Cabadbaran–Santiago forest, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, and Zamboanga del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Sanguila et al., 2016; The Reptile Database, n.d.). Field records from northeastern Mindanao include forest-floor and riparian encounters, including disturbed habitats (Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Taguibo Watershed specimen-associated analysis (Butuan City, eastern Mindanao), this taxon was reported using ground-level habitats in combined riparian and terrestrial-zone records (reported as R. auriculata) (Sanguila et al., 2021). This species reproduces by laying eggs (Uetz et al., 2026).

The back has strongly keeled scales, and a pale stripe crosses the upper lip scales above a pale underside. The Agusan Marsh treatment reports 17 rows of dorsal scales at midbody (Sanguila et al., 2026). The Striped Keelback Snake is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Cabadbaran–Santiago forest, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Taguibo Watershed, Mount Lumot, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). Reported beside lowland freshwater, including some modified environments (Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Taguibo Watershed of Butuan City, the species was found in ground-level habitats (Sanguila et al., 2021). The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

An adult may reach approximately 1.5–2 m body length, making it a large Greater Mindanao snake (Sanguila et al., 2016). Adults reported from the region reached roughly 1.5–2 m (Sanguila et al., 2016). The Müller's Wolf Snake has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Magdiwata, Mount Lumot, Agusan del Norte, and Misamis Oriental. On Samar, records include Mount Huraw and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Müller's Wolf Snake has been recorded in aquatic habitats on northeastern Leyte (Decena et al., 2023). A large individual, about 1.6 m long, was encountered by night partly submerged in a small pool beside a stream in Leyte. A frog was also observed nearby (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The Philippine snake key distinguishes Tropidonophis dendrophiops from T. negrosensis by the number of longitudinal dorsal scale rows counted at the twenty-fifth ventral scale: 17 in T. dendrophiops versus 19 in T. negrosensis (Weinell et al., 2019). This is a comparative scalation character rather than a complete field diagnosis. The Mindanao Spotted Water Snake is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Andanan Watershed Forest Reserve, Mount Lumot, Misamis Oriental, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Supsup et al., 2017). Study records emphasized shaded streams bordered by intact forest (Sanguila et al., 2016). In the Leyte Cordillera and Babatngon ranges, the species was encountered in aquatic microhabitats (Decena et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).

The original description identifies a broad black nuchal patch, beginning several scale rows behind the parietal shields (Uetz et al., 2026). The Southern Triangle-spotted Snake has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Beukema, 2011; GIZ, 2013; Sanguila et al., 2016). The Southern Triangle-spotted Snake is associated with forests. The species lays eggs (Uetz et al., 2026).

records.p: This exceptionally small burrowing snake has a reported maximum total length of 172 mm and differs from related Philippine cyclocorids in body size, scalation and skeletal structure (Weinell et al., 2020). A small burrowing snake with five upper lip scales, 15 longitudinal dorsal scale rows throughout the body and single, undivided subcaudal scales (Uetz et al., 2026). The Waray Drawf Burrowing Snake has been documented on Samar and Leyte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Weinell et al., 2020). The Waray Drawf Burrowing Snake is broadly associated with forests. The anatomical analysis suggested a fossorial lifestyle and probable earthworm feeding, but did not report direct feeding observations (Weinell et al., 2020). Levitonius was described in 2020, with L. mirus recorded from Samar and Leyte. Its diagnosis includes 15 dorsal scale rows, five supralabials and unpaired subcaudal scales (Uetz et al., 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Wildlife Species (OWS).
